title: Gametes, Fertilization and Cleavage
summary: How sperm and eggs are made, how they meet, and how a single zygote divides into a compact ball of cells.

lessons.title: Spermatogenesis and Sperm Maturation

levels.kid:
Inside the body of a grown-up man, there are tiny tubes in the testes. These tubes are like a busy factory that makes sperm cells all day long.

The factory starts with special **starter cells** called stem cells. Some of them copy themselves so the factory never runs out. Others go down the assembly line.

Along the line, each cell splits and changes shape. It gets a head that holds half of the dad's instructions, called DNA. It also grows a long tail for swimming. Helper cells, like nannies, feed and protect the growing cells.

Making one sperm takes about two months. After that, sperm go to a storage tube where they finish growing up and learn to swim well.
levels.hs:
**Spermatogenesis** is the process that makes sperm in the **seminiferous tubules** of the testes. It begins at puberty, when rising hormones switch it on, and continues for life.

The main steps:
- **Spermatogonia** are stem cells near the outer wall of the tubule. They divide by **mitosis**. Some stay as stem cells, and others commit to becoming sperm.
- Committed cells become **primary spermatocytes**, which enter **meiosis**, a special division that halves the chromosome number from 46 to 23.
- After meiosis I they are **secondary spermatocytes**; after meiosis II they are round **spermatids**.
- In **spermiogenesis**, spermatids reshape into sperm. They form a head with tightly packed DNA, an **acrosome** cap full of enzymes, a midpiece packed with mitochondria, and a tail (flagellum).

Large **Sertoli cells** support the developing cells and form the **blood-testis barrier**, which shields them from the immune system. **Leydig cells** between the tubules make **testosterone**.

The whole process takes roughly 64-74 days in humans, and a healthy adult makes millions of sperm per day. Sperm leaving the testis can't yet swim properly. They mature during a journey of about 2 weeks through the **epididymis**, a coiled tube on the back of each testis.
levels.college:
Spermatogenesis runs inside the seminiferous epithelium. Cells move from the basal compartment toward the lumen as they mature.

**Phases**
- **Spermatocytogenesis**: Spermatogonia divide mitotically. Human **A-dark** spermatogonia are considered reserve stem cells, and **A-pale** cells renew and proliferate. A-pale cells give rise to **B spermatogonia**, which become primary spermatocytes.
- **Meiosis**: Primary spermatocytes (2n, 4C) go through a long prophase I, about 3 weeks, in which homologous recombination occurs. Meiosis I gives secondary spermatocytes, which complete meiosis II within hours to form haploid spermatids. One primary spermatocyte yields four spermatids. In oogenesis, by contrast, one cell yields a single egg.
- **Spermiogenesis**: The Golgi builds the **acrosome**, and the centriole nucleates the axoneme (9+2 microtubules). Histones are swapped for transition proteins and then **protamines**, which condense chromatin. Mitochondria wrap the midpiece, and most cytoplasm is shed as a **residual body** that Sertoli cells engulf. Release of the sperm into the lumen is called **spermiation**.

Daughter cells stay linked by **cytoplasmic bridges**, so each clone develops in step and shares gene products.

**Hormonal control (HPG axis)**
- GnRH pulses from the hypothalamus trigger release of LH and FSH.
- **LH** acts on Leydig cells to make testosterone. Testosterone inside the testis is far higher than in blood, and it is essential for spermatogenesis.
- **FSH** acts on Sertoli cells, which respond by making androgen-binding protein and **inhibin B**. Inhibin B feeds back to suppress FSH.

**Sertoli cells** form tight junctions that create the blood-testis barrier. This barrier separates the basal compartment from the adluminal compartment, which holds the later cells. Those later cells carry new surface antigens the immune system has never seen.

**Epididymal maturation**: As sperm pass from the caput to the cauda, they gain progressive motility. Their membrane proteins and lipids are remodeled, they pick up proteins from epididymosomes, and protamine disulfide bonds stabilize the nucleus. The cauda stores sperm. Full ability to fertilize comes later, through capacitation in the female tract.
levels.phd:
**Stem cell kinetics.** The classic human model holds that A-dark spermatogonia are quiescent reserve stem cells and A-pale cells are active renewing progenitors. Single-cell RNA-seq atlases (Guo et al., 2018; Hermann et al., 2018) show a continuum of states instead. A primitive **state 0** is marked by **UTF1, ID4 and FGFR3**, and it progresses toward **KIT-positive** differentiating cells. This has blurred the strict dark/pale split. In the mouse, the stem cell niche depends on Sertoli-derived **GDNF**, which acts through RET/GFRA1, along with FGF2. **Retinoic acid** drives the switch to differentiation by inducing **STRA8**, which is needed for meiotic entry.

**Epithelial cycle.** Heller and Clermont used tritiated thymidine to measure human spermatogenesis at about 64 days, and later estimates run to about 74 days. A cycle of the seminiferous epithelium lasts about 16 days. Humans have **6 stages**, compared with 12 in mice. In humans the stages are arranged in a patchy, partly helical pattern, unlike the neat segmental waves seen in rodents.

**Meiosis.** Prophase I needs **SPO11** to make programmed double-strand breaks. Repair then depends on DMC1/RAD51, and homologs pair through the synaptonemal complex (SYCP1-3). The X and Y chromosomes pair only at the **pseudoautosomal regions**. Unpaired chromatin on the X and Y is silenced in a process called **meiotic sex chromosome inactivation** (MSCI), which forms the XY body. If MSCI fails, cells die at the pachytene checkpoint.

**Chromatin remodeling.** About 85-90% of histones are replaced by PRM1/PRM2, at a ratio near 1:1 in fertile men. The leftover histones are enriched at developmental gene promoters, and some researchers propose this as a route for paternal epigenetic information. Since spermatids are transcriptionally silent during late spermiogenesis, mRNAs are stored and translated later. This storage depends on chromatoid bodies and piRNA-PIWI pathways, which also silence transposons.

**Mutation burden.** Spermatogonia keep dividing for decades, so sperm carry about 80% of de novo point mutations, and that number rises by about 1-2 mutations per year of paternal age (Kong et al., 2012). **Selfish spermatogonial selection** gives an extra advantage to clones with FGFR2/FGFR3 gain-of-function mutations, which helps explain the paternal age effect in achondroplasia and Apert syndrome.
levels.expert:
**Clinical evaluation.** Male factor contributes to about half of infertile couples. The WHO 2021 manual (6th edition) gives lower reference limits, set at the 5th centile of fertile men: concentration about 16 million/mL, progressive motility 30%, and normal forms 4% under strict Kruger criteria. These are reference limits, not diagnostic cutoffs. Results vary a lot between samples, so at least two analyses are needed.

**Azoospermia** can be obstructive (normal spermatogenesis, as with congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens linked to CFTR variants) or non-obstructive (failure of spermatogenesis). Elevated FSH alongside low inhibin B points to failure inside the testis. Genetic workup includes a karyotype, which can show Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY), the most common chromosomal cause, and screening for **Y-chromosome AZF microdeletions**. Deletions of AZFa or AZFb predict that no sperm will be found by surgery. AZFc deletions often leave retrievable sperm. In non-obstructive azoospermia, **micro-TESE** finds sperm in roughly half of men by targeting islands of active tubules. Those sperm are then used with ICSI, which can pass AZF deletions on to sons.

**Pharmacology pitfalls.** Exogenous testosterone and anabolic steroids suppress LH and FSH through negative feedback. This collapses testosterone levels inside the testis and can cause azoospermia, while blood testosterone looks normal. Recovery can take months. Other threats to spermatogenesis include:
- Alkylating chemotherapy, especially cyclophosphamide, and pelvic radiation, which can permanently deplete stem cells. Sperm banking before treatment is standard of care.
- Sulfasalazine, which reversibly lowers sperm count and quality.
- 5-alpha reductase inhibitors and opioids (through hypogonadism), which can also impair it.

Any cause has a delayed effect because the whole process of making sperm takes about 2.5 months.

**DNA fragmentation** tests (SCSA, TUNEL) measure sperm DNA damage, which is linked to oxidative stress and varicocele. Their value in guiding treatment is still debated.

**Frontiers.** Researchers are working on:
- **Spermatogonial stem cell transplantation** for prepubertal cancer survivors. Testicular tissue is cryopreserved now and could be transplanted back later. Orwig's group showed this in macaques, which produced offspring.
- In vitro spermatogenesis, achieved in mice and still incomplete in humans.
- Male contraceptives. Examples include NES/testosterone gel, which suppresses gonadotropins, soluble adenylyl cyclase inhibitors such as TDI-11861 that block sperm motility on demand, and retinoic acid signalling blockers.

keyPoints: Spermatogenesis occurs in seminiferous tubules from puberty onward, taking about 64-74 days
Spermatogonia (mitosis) become spermatocytes (meiosis), then spermatids
Spermiogenesis builds the acrosome, flagellum and protamine-packed head
Sertoli cells nurse germ cells and form the blood-testis barrier; Leydig cells make testosterone
LH drives Leydig testosterone; FSH acts on Sertoli cells; inhibin B suppresses FSH
Sperm gain motility in the epididymis; ongoing divisions drive the paternal age mutation effect

test.q: Where in the testis does spermatogenesis take place?
test.explain: Germ cells develop into sperm within the epithelium of the seminiferous tubules. The epididymis matures sperm but does not make them. The rete testis and vas deferens carry sperm but do not produce them.

test.q: Which cell type undergoes meiosis I?
test.explain: Primary spermatocytes enter meiosis I. Type B spermatogonia divide by mitosis to produce primary spermatocytes. Elongating spermatids are already haploid. Sertoli cells are somatic support cells that do not undergo meiosis.

test.q: How many spermatids come from one primary spermatocyte?
test.explain: Two meiotic divisions yield four haploid spermatids.

test.q: Which hormone acts on Leydig cells to stimulate testosterone production?
test.explain: LH targets Leydig cells. FSH acts on Sertoli cells instead.

test.q: What is the main role of the blood-testis barrier?
choices: Shielding later germ cells from immunity
test.explain: Sertoli tight junctions protect later germ cells, which carry antigens the immune system has never seen.

test.q: During spermiogenesis, histones are largely replaced by:
test.explain: Protamines tightly condense sperm DNA into the small head.

test.q: Where do sperm gain progressive motility?
test.explain: Motility develops during transit from the caput to the cauda of the epididymis.

test.q: The sperm midpiece is packed with which organelle?
test.explain: Mitochondria wrap the midpiece and supply energy for the tail.

test.q: Inhibin B from Sertoli cells mainly suppresses:
test.explain: Inhibin B gives negative feedback on FSH secretion.

test.q: The enzyme-filled cap over the sperm head, built by the Golgi, is the ___.
test.explain: The acrosome forms from the Golgi apparatus during spermiogenesis.

test.q: What are the stem cells near the base of the seminiferous tubule called?
test.explain: Spermatogonia renew themselves and also produce committed cells.

test.q: The transformation of round spermatids into shaped sperm is called ___.
test.explain: Spermiogenesis is the reshaping phase. It involves no cell division.

kidTest.q: Where are sperm made?
kidTest.explain: Tiny tubes in the testes are the sperm factory.

kidTest.q: What does the sperm's tail help it do?
kidTest.explain: The long tail is for swimming.

kidTest.q: What does the sperm's head hold?
kidTest.explain: The head carries half of the dad's instructions.

kidTest.q: About how long does it take to make one sperm?
kidTest.explain: It takes about two months.

kidTest.q: Helper cells feed growing sperm like a n _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: Helper cells care for the growing sperm like nannies.

advancedTest.q: A man using exogenous testosterone has normal blood testosterone but azoospermia. The best explanation is:
choices: Testosterone directly kills spermatogonia through oxidative damage
Gonadotropin suppression lowers testosterone inside the testis
The blood-testis barrier stops testosterone from reaching germ cells
Androgen receptors in the testis become desensitized to high hormone levels
advancedTest.explain: Negative feedback suppresses LH and FSH, so Leydig cells stop making the high testosterone levels needed inside the testis.

advancedTest.q: Why does the paternal age effect exist for de novo point mutations?
choices: Older men produce more abnormal meiotic recombination in prophase I
Sperm DNA is repaired much less well once protamine packing begins
Epididymal transit grows longer with age and damages stored sperm DNA
Spermatogonia keep dividing for decades, adding replication errors
advancedTest.explain: Ongoing stem cell mitoses build up errors. Selfish FGFR mutations add a further clonal advantage.

advancedTest.q: A non-obstructive azoospermic man has an AZFb deletion. The best counseling is:
choices: The deletion can be reversed by FSH therapy before retrieval
Micro-TESE is very likely to find sperm for use with ICSI
Sperm retrieval is unlikely, so surgery is usually not advised
AZFb deletions mainly cause obstruction, so surgery is curative
advancedTest.explain: AZFa and AZFb deletions predict that no sperm will be retrieved. AZFc deletions often leave retrievable sperm.

advancedTest.q: If meiotic sex chromosome inactivation fails in a spermatocyte, the expected result is:
choices: Cell death at the pachytene checkpoint
Aneuploid sperm that fertilize at normal rates
advancedTest.explain: Failure of MSCI triggers death at the pachytene checkpoint, which removes the defective spermatocytes.

lessons.title: Oogenesis, Meiotic Arrest and Folliculogenesis

levels.kid:
Before a baby girl is even born, tiny egg cells are already growing inside her. By about halfway through her time in the womb, she has millions of them!

Then something surprising happens. Each egg starts to get ready, and then it presses "pause." It can stay paused for many years, like a movie stopped in the middle.

Each egg lives inside a little bubble of helper cells called a **follicle**. The helpers feed the egg and talk to it, like a nest around a bird egg.

Most eggs never finish. Only about 400 ever get released in a whole lifetime. Every month after a girl grows up, one egg presses "play" again and gets ready to leave.
levels.hs:
**Oogenesis** is the making of eggs (oocytes). Unlike sperm, which are made all through adult life, eggs are started before birth.

The steps:
- **Primordial germ cells** travel to the developing ovary and become **oogonia**, which multiply by mitosis.
- Around month 5 of fetal life, there are about 7 million. Many then die off. About 1 to 2 million remain at birth, and roughly 400,000 at puberty.
- Oogonia enter **meiosis**, the special division that halves the chromosome number. They become **primary oocytes** but stop partway through, in **prophase I**. This pause, called **meiotic arrest**, can last from before birth until ovulation, up to about 50 years.

Each oocyte sits in a **follicle**, surrounded by support cells called **granulosa cells**. **Folliculogenesis** is the growth of follicles: primordial, then primary, then secondary, and finally a large fluid-filled **antral (Graafian) follicle**.

At each cycle after puberty, a hormone surge restarts meiosis in one oocyte. It finishes meiosis I and pauses again, now as a **secondary oocyte** at metaphase II. Meiosis II finishes only if a sperm fertilizes it.

A real example: because eggs wait so long, errors in separating chromosomes become more common with age. This is why **Down syndrome** (an extra chromosome 21) becomes more likely as maternal age rises.
levels.college:
**Origin.** Primordial germ cells arise in the epiblast, move to the yolk sac wall, then migrate along the hindgut to the gonadal ridges by about week 5. In an XX gonad, they become **oogonia** and proliferate mitotically. They remain connected by cytoplasmic bridges, forming clusters (nests).

**Entry into meiosis.** From about week 11 to 12, oogonia enter meiosis I. **Retinoic acid** induces **STRA8**, the gatekeeper of meiotic entry. Cells pass through leptotene, zygotene and pachytene, where homologs synapse and cross over, then arrest at **diplotene** (the **dictyate stage**). They are now **primary oocytes**.

**Numbers.** Germ cells peak near 6 to 7 million at about 20 weeks. Massive **atresia** (apoptosis) leaves about 1 to 2 million at birth. No new oocytes are made after birth, by the classic view.

**Follicle stages:**
- **Primordial**: oocyte plus one flat layer of pregranulosa cells. These form the resting reserve.
- **Primary**: granulosa cells become cuboidal, and the **zona pellucida** (glycoproteins ZP1 to ZP4) forms.
- **Secondary (preantral)**: multiple granulosa layers. **Theca interna** cells appear outside the basement membrane.
- **Antral/Graafian**: a fluid-filled antrum forms. The oocyte sits on a stalk of cells, the **cumulus oophorus**.

**Hormones.** Early growth does not depend on gonadotropins. Antral growth depends on **FSH**. In the **two-cell model**, LH drives theca cells to make androgens, and FSH drives granulosa **aromatase** to convert them to estradiol. One dominant follicle is usually selected each cycle.

**Resumption.** The **LH surge** triggers germinal vesicle breakdown and completion of meiosis I. Division is very unequal: it yields a large **secondary oocyte** and a tiny **first polar body**. The oocyte then arrests at **metaphase II** until fertilization.
levels.phd:
**Maintaining prophase I arrest.** In the dictyate oocyte, cyclic AMP stays high. The oocyte membrane receptor **GPR3** activates Gs and adenylyl cyclase. The granulosa cells add **cGMP**, made by the receptor **NPR2** when stimulated by C-type natriuretic peptide (**CNP**). This cGMP diffuses into the oocyte through **gap junctions** made of connexin 37 and 43. There it inhibits the enzyme **PDE3A**, so cAMP is not broken down. High cAMP activates **PKA**, which keeps **CDK1/cyclin B** (maturation-promoting factor, MPF) inactive. It does this through WEE1B, which adds inhibitory phosphates, and by restraining CDC25B, which would remove them.

**Release by LH.** LH acts on mural granulosa cells, not on the oocyte, which lacks LH receptors. Through EGF-like ligands (amphiregulin, epiregulin) and EGFR signalling, CNP and NPR2 activity fall and gap junctions close. Oocyte cGMP drops, PDE3A becomes active, and cAMP falls. MPF activates and the nuclear envelope (germinal vesicle) breaks down. Cumulus cells expand by building a **hyaluronan** matrix.

**Metaphase II arrest.** This arrest is held by **cytostatic factor**. Its key part is **EMI2**, which inhibits the APC/C (anaphase-promoting complex) and so keeps cyclin B stable. Sperm-triggered calcium oscillations later release this block.

**Bidirectional dialogue.** The oocyte is not passive. It secretes **GDF9** and **BMP15**, which drive granulosa proliferation and cumulus function. Granulosa cells supply metabolites the oocyte cannot make well, such as pyruvate and amino acids, through gap junctions. In mice, *Gdf9* knockout blocks follicle growth at the primary stage.

**Primordial follicle activation.** The resting state depends on **PTEN** and **FOXO3** restraining PI3K–AKT signalling. Deleting PTEN in oocytes activates the entire pool at once and causes premature ovarian failure in mice (Reddy et al., 2008). **AMH** from growing follicles slows further recruitment.

**Controversy.** The dogma of a fixed oocyte pool was challenged by Johnson et al. (2004), who reported putative **oogonial stem cells**. The idea remains contested, and most evidence suggests they make little or no contribution to normal human fertility.
levels.expert:
**Maternal age and aneuploidy.** Most human trisomies come from maternal meiosis I errors. The leading explanation is **age-related loss of cohesin**. The meiosis-specific cohesin subunits (REC8, SMC1β) are loaded in fetal life and are barely renewed. Over decades, cohesion between sister chromatids weakens. Crossovers drift toward chromosome ends, homologs separate early, and chromatids are mis-segregated. Human oocytes are also unusually error-prone even when young. The spindle assembles slowly and lacks centrosomes, and the spindle assembly checkpoint is permissive with a large cytoplasm. Aneuploidy rates in eggs rise steeply after the mid-30s. This is why preimplantation genetic testing of embryos (PGT-A) is debated: mosaic embryos complicate interpretation.

**Reserve assessment.** Serum **AMH** and the **antral follicle count** on ultrasound estimate the size of the growing pool. They predict how the ovaries will respond to stimulation, not egg quality or the chance of natural conception. This is a frequent counselling pitfall.

**Clinical correlates:**
- **Turner syndrome (45,X)**: oocytes are lost rapidly, giving "streak" ovaries.
- **FMR1 premutation**: carriers have a 55 to 200 CGG repeat expansion and are at risk of premature ovarian insufficiency.
- **Gonadotoxic chemotherapy** (especially alkylating agents) depletes the primordial pool. Fertility preservation options include egg cryopreservation and ovarian tissue freezing with later regrafting.
- **PCOS**: there is an excess of small antral follicles with high AMH, androgen excess, and failed dominant follicle selection.
- **Oocyte maturation arrest**: an infertility phenotype linked to variants in genes such as *TUBB8* and *PATL2*.

**IVF translation.** Eggs removed from follicles mature on their own, because removal cuts off the cGMP supply from granulosa cells. This led to **in vitro maturation (IVM)** protocols. "Biphasic" IVM uses CNP to hold meiotic arrest first, so that nuclear and cytoplasmic maturity stay in step. The "dual trigger" (GnRH agonist plus hCG) plays on the LH-surge biology of meiotic resumption.

**Frontiers.** Hayashi's group generated functional mouse eggs entirely in vitro from stem cells. In 2023 they made eggs from male mouse cells. Human in vitro gametogenesis can now reach oogonia-like cells but not mature eggs. **Mitochondrial replacement** techniques target mtDNA disease transmitted through the egg. Open questions remain on how the epigenetic imprints set during oocyte growth stay faithful in vitro.

keyPoints: Oogenesis begins before birth; oogonia multiply by mitosis and peak near 7 million at 20 weeks
Primary oocytes arrest in prophase I (dictyate/diplotene) until ovulation, up to decades
Follicles progress: primordial, primary, secondary, antral (Graafian)
The LH surge restarts meiosis; the secondary oocyte arrests at metaphase II until fertilization
Granulosa cGMP through gap junctions keeps oocyte cAMP high and MPF off
Cohesin loss with age drives maternal meiotic errors such as trisomy 21

test.q: At what stage are primary oocytes arrested from fetal life until puberty or later?
test.explain: Primary oocytes stop in prophase I (diplotene/dictyate). Metaphase II arrest comes later, in the secondary oocyte.

test.q: Roughly how many germ cells are in the ovaries at their peak, around 20 weeks of fetal life?
test.explain: Germ cells peak at about 6 to 7 million mid-gestation. Atresia leaves about 1 to 2 million at birth.

test.q: Which follicle stage first shows a fluid-filled cavity?
test.explain: The antrum defines the antral (Graafian) follicle. Primordial and primary follicles have no fluid space.

test.q: What event restarts meiosis I in the oocyte each cycle?
test.explain: The LH surge triggers completion of meiosis I. Sperm entry completes meiosis II, not meiosis I.

test.q: Completing meiosis I yields a secondary oocyte plus a:
test.explain: Meiosis I division is very unequal. Most of the cytoplasm stays in the oocyte, and the extra chromosomes go into a tiny polar body.

test.q: In the two-cell model, aromatase in granulosa cells converts theca androgens into:
test.explain: FSH-driven granulosa aromatase converts androgens made by LH-stimulated theca cells into estradiol.

test.q: Which structure first forms around the oocyte at the primary follicle stage?
test.explain: The zona pellucida, a glycoprotein coat made of ZP1 to ZP4, appears as the follicle becomes primary.

test.q: Why does risk of trisomy 21 rise with maternal age?
test.explain: Long meiotic arrest allows chromosome-segregation errors to accumulate. The classic view holds that no new eggs are made after birth.

test.q: Which hormone mainly drives growth of antral follicles?
test.explain: Early follicle growth does not need gonadotropins, but antral growth depends on follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH).

test.q: The apoptotic death of oocytes and follicles is called ___.
test.explain: Atresia removes most germ cells. Only about 400 oocytes are ever ovulated.

test.q: What are the support cells immediately surrounding the oocyte inside a follicle called?
test.explain: Granulosa cells nourish and signal to the oocyte. Theca cells lie outside the basement membrane.

test.q: Fetal germ cells that multiply by mitosis before entering meiosis are called ___.
test.explain: Oogonia divide mitotically, then enter meiosis I to become primary oocytes.

kidTest.q: When do a girl's egg cells start to form?
kidTest.explain: Eggs begin forming while she is still growing in the womb.

kidTest.q: What does a growing egg do for many years?
kidTest.explain: Each egg presses pause partway through getting ready.

kidTest.q: What do the helper cells around an egg do?
kidTest.explain: Helper cells in the follicle feed the egg and send it signals.

kidTest.q: About how many eggs get released in a whole lifetime?
kidTest.explain: Out of millions, only about 400 are ever released.

kidTest.q: The little bubble of helper cells around an egg is a f _ _ _ _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: A follicle is the egg's nest of helper cells.

advancedTest.q: A drug that blocks gap junctions between granulosa cells and a dictyate oocyte would most likely:
choices: Strengthen prophase I arrest by raising oocyte cAMP
Block germinal vesicle breakdown by inhibiting CDK1
Trigger meiotic resumption by lowering oocyte cGMP
Arrest the oocyte at metaphase II through EMI2
advancedTest.explain: Granulosa cGMP inhibits PDE3A only if it reaches the oocyte. Cutting the supply frees PDE3A, lowers cAMP and activates MPF, much as LH does.

advancedTest.q: Oocyte-specific deletion of PTEN in mice causes premature ovarian failure because:
choices: Cohesin is lost prematurely from oocyte chromosomes
Granulosa cells stop secreting anti-Müllerian hormone
FOXO3 becomes overactive and kills resting oocytes
PI3K–AKT activation recruits the primordial pool at once
advancedTest.explain: PTEN restrains PI3K–AKT. Without it, FOXO3 is inactivated and all primordial follicles activate, so the reserve is used up.

advancedTest.q: A patient has a low AMH level. Which counselling statement is best supported?
choices: Ovarian response to stimulation may be reduced
Her oocytes are likely to be aneuploid
Natural conception this year is unlikely
advancedTest.explain: AMH reflects the size of the growing follicle pool and predicts stimulation response. It does not measure egg quality or natural fertility.

advancedTest.q: Why do maternal-age trisomies arise mainly in meiosis I?
choices: Metaphase II arrest lasts decades and erodes the spindle
Fetal-loaded cohesin decays, weakening chiasma maintenance
Spermatocytes contribute more extra chromosomes with age
Granulosa cGMP rises with age and stalls segregation
advancedTest.explain: REC8-containing cohesin is loaded before birth and barely renewed. Its loss over decades destabilizes homolog attachment at meiosis I. Metaphase II arrest lasts only hours to days.

lessons.title: Ovulation, Sperm Transport and Capacitation

levels.kid:
Once a month, one of a woman's two **ovaries** lets go of a single tiny egg. This is called **ovulation**. The egg floats into a soft tube, like a slide, that leads toward the womb.

Meanwhile, sperm cells have a very long trip. For something so tiny, it is like swimming across a huge lake. Most sperm get lost or tired along the way. Only a few hundred ever reach the egg.

Here is a cool secret. Sperm are not ready to meet the egg right away. They have to "warm up" inside the woman's body first, a bit like a runner stretching before a race. Scientists call this warm-up **capacitation**. After it, the sperm swim harder and are ready for the big moment.
levels.hs:
**Ovulation** is the release of a mature egg (technically a **secondary oocyte**) from the ovary. It is triggered by a sharp spike of **luteinizing hormone (LH)** from the pituitary gland, called the **LH surge**. About a day and a half after the surge begins, the ripe follicle bursts. The oocyte comes out wrapped in a cloud of helper cells called the **cumulus**. Finger-like fringes on the end of the uterine tube, the **fimbriae**, sweep it inside. The egg stays able to be fertilized for roughly 12 to 24 hours.

**Sperm transport** is a filtering journey. Hundreds of millions of sperm are deposited in the vagina, but the acidic environment, cervical mucus, the uterus and the narrow tube entrance remove most of them. Only a few hundred reach the **ampulla**, the wide part of the tube where fertilization usually happens. Muscle contractions in the uterus help move sperm along, not just their own swimming.

**Capacitation** is a set of changes sperm must go through inside the female tract before they can fertilize. Freshly ejaculated sperm cannot fertilize an egg. Over several hours, cholesterol is stripped from their membranes, and their tails start beating in a strong, whip-like pattern called **hyperactivation**.

Real example: in IVF labs, sperm are incubated in a special medium before being added to eggs. This lets capacitation happen outside the body.
levels.college:
**Ovulation.** Rising estradiol from the dominant follicle switches the hypothalamic-pituitary axis from negative to **positive feedback**. The result is the mid-cycle **LH surge**. The surge has several effects:
- It restarts meiosis I in the oocyte, which then completes it, extrudes the first polar body and arrests at metaphase II.
- It drives **cumulus expansion**. Cumulus cells secrete hyaluronan, organized by proteins such as TSG-6.
- It triggers proteolysis of the follicle wall, involving prostaglandins, plasmin and matrix metalloproteinases.

Ovulation occurs about 36 hours after surge onset, or about 10-12 hours after the LH peak. The ruptured follicle becomes the progesterone-secreting **corpus luteum**.

**Oocyte pickup and tubal transport.** The fimbriae grip the cumulus-oocyte complex using ciliary beating. Cilia and smooth muscle then carry it to the ampulla.

**Sperm transport.** Sperm move in two phases:
- **Rapid phase:** within minutes, uterine contractions carry some sperm to the tubes. These early arrivals are usually not yet fertilization-competent.
- **Sustained phase:** sperm enter cervical crypts and are released gradually.

At the **uterotubal junction** and lower **isthmus**, sperm bind to the epithelium and form a **reservoir**. This storage keeps sperm alive and slows capacitation, so sperm are available for several days. Only about 1 in a million of the ejaculated sperm reaches the ampulla.

**Capacitation** was discovered independently by **Chang** and **Austin** in 1951. Its key events:
- Albumin in tubal fluid removes membrane cholesterol, which makes the membrane more fluid.
- HCO3⁻ enters and activates **soluble adenylyl cyclase (sAC/ADCY10)**. This raises cAMP and activates PKA.
- PKA starts a cascade that ends in tyrosine phosphorylation of many proteins.
- Intracellular pH rises and Ca²⁺ flows in through **CatSper** channels, producing **hyperactivated motility**.

Capacitation gets the sperm ready for the acrosome reaction, which is covered in the next lesson.
levels.phd:
**LH signaling paradox.** LH receptors sit mainly on mural granulosa and theca cells, not on the oocyte or cumulus. The ovulatory signal therefore has to be relayed inward. **Conti and colleagues** showed that LH induces the EGF-like ligands **amphiregulin, epiregulin and betacellulin**, which act on EGFR in cumulus cells. EGFR signaling lowers cGMP in the cumulus. Before the surge, cGMP had diffused through gap junctions into the oocyte, where it inhibited PDE3A and kept cAMP high, holding the oocyte in prophase I arrest. Once cGMP falls, PDE3A degrades oocyte cAMP, MPF activates, and meiosis resumes. Cumulus expansion needs COX-2-derived PGE2 and an oocyte-secreted signal (GDF9/BMP15). The hyaluronan matrix is cross-linked by the heavy chains of serum inter-α-inhibitor, with TSG-6 and pentraxin-3 acting as catalysts.

**Reservoir biology.** Isthmic binding depends on sperm-head proteins. In some species these include BSP proteins acquired from seminal plasma, along with glycan recognition (for example, Lewis-X and sialylated motifs in some species). At ovulation, sperm are released as hyperactivation develops and the binding molecules are remodeled. Human sperm that are capacitated at any given moment form a small, transient, rotating subpopulation. This argues against a single synchronous event.

**Molecular core of capacitation.** The main steps:
- Cholesterol efflux to albumin and HDL.
- HCO3⁻ entry via SLC26 transporters and NBC co-transporters.
- Activation of sAC (ADCY10), then PKA, which leads to Src-family kinase and tyrosine phosphorylation.
- Hyperpolarization via **SLO3** K⁺ channels.
- Alkalinization via the **Hv1** proton channel, which is prominent in human sperm.

**CatSper** is a principal-piece Ca²⁺ channel complex with more than ten subunits. Lishko, Kirichok and Strünker showed that, in humans, it is directly activated by **progesterone** through the lipid hydrolase **ABHD2**. Progesterone is released by cumulus cells.

**Guidance.** Several mechanisms have been proposed to steer sperm toward the egg:
- **Rheotaxis:** swimming against fluid flow, a robust effect.
- **Thermotaxis:** following a roughly 1-2 °C rise toward the ampulla.
- **Chemotaxis:** following chemical gradients, possibly progesterone.

The physiological importance of each in humans is still contested, as is the debated role of olfactory receptors such as OR1D2.
levels.expert:
**Clinical exploitation of the LH surge.** Urinary LH kits detect the surge, so intercourse or insemination can be timed within the roughly 6-day fertile window. Probability of conception peaks in the 1-2 days before ovulation (Wilcox et al., NEJM 1995), not after it. This matches a sperm reservoir that outlives the brief viability of the oocyte. In IVF, a "trigger" is given and oocytes are retrieved about 34-36 hours later, just before predicted rupture. Using a **GnRH-agonist trigger** to release endogenous LH, instead of hCG, markedly reduces ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome. This works because the agonist-induced surge is shorter, which limits luteal VEGF. A rare pitfall is **empty follicle syndrome**. "Genuine" cases have been linked to LHCGR variants; many apparent cases reflect trigger failures.

**Anovulation and luteinized unruptured follicle.** In luteinized unruptured follicle (LUF) syndrome, progesterone rises without rupture. As a result, a mid-luteal progesterone level does not prove that ovulation occurred. LUF has been associated with NSAID use, since rupture depends on prostaglandins. Selective COX-2 inhibitors delay rupture in human studies, which highlights PGE2 as a non-hormonal contraceptive target.

**Sperm failure modes.** Several defects block transport or capacitation:
- **CATSPER1/2** mutations cause male infertility with normal semen counts but absent hyperactivation. The cause is invisible on a routine semen analysis.
- Deletions in the **CATSPER2-STRC** region also cause hearing loss (deafness-infertility syndrome).
- Recessive **ADCY10** variants cause asthenozoospermia.
- Hostile cervical mucus and antisperm antibodies impair cervical passage. Intrauterine insemination bypasses the cervix.
- **ICSI** bypasses capacitation-dependent steps entirely. This is why CatSper-null sperm can still produce embryos with it.

**Pharmacology frontiers.** CatSper, SLO3 and sAC are attractive male/on-demand contraceptive targets because they are essential for sperm function (CatSper and SLO3 are sperm-specific). **TDI-11861**, a sAC inhibitor, reversibly immobilized mouse sperm and prevented pregnancy (Balbach et al., 2023). Progesterone and prostaglandin activation of CatSper also means environmental chemicals that hit the channel, including some UV filters and plasticizers, could act as "sperm disruptors."

**Open questions.** Several key problems remain unresolved:
- How is capacitation timed in vivo to match ovulation?
- Is the decapacitation by seminal factors physiologically reversible?
- Which human guidance mechanisms are essential?
- Why do human IVF media trigger capacitation that only partially mimics the tube?

keyPoints: An estradiol-triggered LH surge causes ovulation about 36 hours after surge onset
The ovulated oocyte is arrested at metaphase II inside an expanded cumulus
Fimbriae capture the oocyte; fertilization usually occurs in the ampulla
Sperm are filtered from millions to hundreds and stored in an isthmic reservoir
Capacitation: cholesterol loss, HCO3- and sAC/cAMP/PKA, tyrosine phosphorylation
CatSper Ca2+ entry, activated by progesterone in humans, drives hyperactivation

test.q: Which hormonal event directly triggers ovulation?
choices: A sharp rise in serum prolactin
A steep drop in serum FSH levels
A sudden fall in serum progesterone
test.explain: The mid-cycle LH surge, caused by estradiol switching to positive feedback, triggers follicle rupture about 36 hours after surge onset.

test.q: At what stage is the human oocyte arrested when it is ovulated?
test.explain: After the LH surge the oocyte completes meiosis I, extrudes a polar body, and arrests at metaphase II until fertilization.

test.q: Where in the uterine tube does fertilization usually take place?
test.explain: The ampulla is the wide segment where fertilization usually happens; the isthmus holds the sperm reservoir.

test.q: What structure becomes the corpus luteum?
choices: The cumulus cells around the egg
test.explain: After ovulation the remaining follicle cells form the progesterone-secreting corpus luteum.

test.q: What is the main role of the sperm reservoir at the isthmus?
test.explain: Binding to isthmic epithelium keeps sperm alive and slows capacitation, so sperm are available for days.

test.q: Which change in the sperm membrane is an early step of capacitation?
test.explain: Albumin removes cholesterol from the sperm membrane, increasing fluidity and starting the signaling cascade.

test.q: Which enzyme is activated by bicarbonate during capacitation?
test.explain: HCO3- activates soluble adenylyl cyclase (sAC/ADCY10), raising cAMP and activating PKA.

test.q: The CatSper channel lets which ion into sperm?
test.explain: CatSper is a Ca2+ channel in the sperm tail; calcium entry drives hyperactivated motility.

test.q: Sperm that reach the tubes within minutes are typically:
test.explain: The rapid transport phase moves sperm fast, but these early arrivals usually have not completed capacitation.

test.q: The finger-like fringes that sweep the egg into the uterine tube are called ___.
test.explain: The fimbriae capture the cumulus-oocyte complex using ciliary beating.

test.q: What is the strong, whip-like tail beating that develops during capacitation called?
test.explain: Hyperactivation is the high-amplitude, asymmetric flagellar beat that helps sperm detach and penetrate egg coverings.

test.q: Capacitation was discovered independently in 1951 by Chang and ___.
test.explain: M.C. Chang and C.R. Austin independently showed that sperm need time in the female tract to fertilize.

kidTest.q: What happens during ovulation?
choices: The ovary lets go of an egg
kidTest.explain: Ovulation is when an ovary releases an egg.

kidTest.q: About how many sperm reach the egg?
kidTest.explain: Most sperm get lost; only a few hundred make it.

kidTest.q: Where does the egg go after it leaves the ovary?
kidTest.explain: The egg moves into the uterine tube that leads toward the womb.

kidTest.q: Capacitation is a bit like a runner who is:
kidTest.explain: Sperm need a warm-up inside the body before they are ready.

kidTest.q: The egg is made in an organ called the o _ _ _ y.
kidTest.explain: The ovary stores and releases eggs.

advancedTest.q: LH receptors sit mostly on mural granulosa cells, yet meiosis resumes in the oocyte. What best explains this?
choices: Cumulus hyaluronan sends calcium waves that directly start metaphase I
Progesterone from the corpus luteum activates oocyte maturation factor
LH crosses the zona and binds oocyte nuclear receptors
EGF-like ligands lower cumulus cGMP, letting oocyte PDE3A destroy cAMP
advancedTest.explain: LH induces amphiregulin and related ligands; EGFR signaling reduces cGMP flow through gap junctions, releasing PDE3A inhibition so cAMP falls and MPF activates.

advancedTest.q: A man has normal sperm count and morphology but infertility; his sperm cannot hyperactivate. IVF fails but ICSI succeeds. Which defect fits best?
advancedTest.explain: CatSper loss abolishes Ca2+-driven hyperactivation without affecting routine semen parameters, and ICSI bypasses the need for it.

advancedTest.q: Conception probability peaks 1-2 days before ovulation rather than after. Which explanation is most consistent?
choices: The oocyte is most fertile before rupture occurs
The LH surge itself directly capacitates sperm
Cervical mucus blocks sperm after ovulation begins
Sperm stored in a reservoir outlive the brief oocyte lifespan
advancedTest.explain: The oocyte is viable only about a day, while reservoir sperm survive days, so sperm present beforehand are best placed to fertilize.

advancedTest.q: Why does a progesterone rise not reliably prove that ovulation occurred?
choices: Progesterone falls sharply right after the LH peak
Luteinized follicles can secrete it without rupturing
Progesterone is made by sperm in the tube
Estradiol replaces progesterone after a true ovulation
advancedTest.explain: In luteinized unruptured follicle syndrome the follicle luteinizes and makes progesterone but never releases the oocyte.

lessons.title: Fertilization: Acrosome Reaction, Zona Binding and Polyspermy Blocks

levels.kid:
Imagine a castle with a thick jelly wall around it. Inside is the egg. Many tiny swimmers, the sperm, race to get in, but only one is allowed.

Each sperm carries a little bag of special scissors on its head. When it reaches the jelly wall, the bag opens. The scissors help the sperm cut a path through the wall.

When the first sperm touches the egg, the two join together. Right away, the egg sends out a signal that makes the wall turn hard, like a gate slamming shut. Now no other sperm can get in.

Why does that matter? The egg needs exactly one set of instructions from the dad. Two sets would be too many, and the baby could not grow properly.
levels.hs:
**Fertilization** is the joining of one sperm and one egg (oocyte) to make a **zygote**, the first cell of a new person. It usually happens in the widest part of the fallopian tube, called the **ampulla**.

The egg is surrounded by two barriers:
- The **corona radiata**, a layer of follicle cells held together by a sticky substance called hyaluronan.
- The **zona pellucida**, a thick, clear coat made of glycoproteins (proteins with sugars attached).

The front of the sperm head contains a cap called the **acrosome**, which is full of enzymes. When the sperm binds the zona pellucida, the acrosome releases these enzymes. This is the **acrosome reaction**. The enzymes, along with strong tail beating, let the sperm drill through the zona. The sperm then fuses with the egg's cell membrane.

Only one sperm should enter. If two get in, the result is **polyspermy**, which gives the cell three sets of chromosomes (triploidy). Triploid embryos usually do not survive. To prevent this, sperm entry triggers a wave of calcium inside the egg. Small packets just under the egg's surface, called **cortical granules**, then release enzymes that change the zona so other sperm cannot bind. This is the **zona reaction**.

The calcium wave also wakes the egg up. It finishes its second meiotic division, and the sperm and egg nuclei become **pronuclei** that soon combine their chromosomes.
levels.college:
Fertilization in humans occurs in the **ampulla** of the uterine tube, usually within roughly a day of ovulation. Only capacitated sperm can take part.

**Crossing the corona radiata.** Sperm push through the cumulus cells, helped by the membrane hyaluronidase **PH-20 (SPAM1)** and **hyperactivated motility** driven by the sperm-specific calcium channel **CatSper**.

**Zona binding.** The human zona pellucida has four glycoproteins: **ZP1, ZP2, ZP3 and ZP4**. ZP2 forms the structural filaments, cross-linked by ZP1. Older mouse work named ZP3 as the primary sperm receptor. Current evidence shows that the N-terminal domain of **ZP2** is essential for sperm binding in both mice and humans.

**Acrosome reaction.** The acrosome is a Golgi-derived exocytotic vesicle. Calcium influx causes the outer acrosomal membrane to fuse with the plasma membrane at many points, releasing **acrosin** (a serine protease) and other hydrolases. This also exposes the inner acrosomal membrane, which carries the fusion protein **IZUMO1**. The protein-cutting enzymes and the mechanical thrust of the tail together cut a narrow channel through the zona.

**Gamete fusion.** IZUMO1 binds **JUNO** (folate receptor 4) on the egg membrane. The egg tetraspanin **CD9** is also required. The sperm's equatorial segment fuses first, and the whole sperm nucleus enters the egg.

**Egg activation.** The sperm delivers **phospholipase C zeta (PLCζ)**. PLCζ produces IP3, which triggers repeated **calcium oscillations**. These oscillations cause three things:
- **Cortical granule exocytosis**
- Completion of **meiosis II**, which releases the second polar body
- Formation of the **pronuclei** and the start of embryonic metabolism

**Polyspermy blocks.**
- Many species have a **fast electrical block** (membrane depolarization). Mammals lack a meaningful version.
- The **slow block**, or **zona reaction**: the cortical granule protease **ovastacin** cleaves ZP2, so the zona stops binding sperm and hardens.
- A **membrane block**: JUNO is quickly shed from the egg surface after fusion.
levels.phd:
The mechanism of mammalian sperm-zona recognition has changed substantially over the past few decades. Wassarman's classic mouse experiments proposed that O-linked glycans on **ZP3** bind sperm and trigger the acrosome reaction. Later genetic work by Dean's group largely overturned this model. Mouse eggs carrying human ZP2 bind human sperm, and sperm still bound zonae with mutated ZP3. When the ZP2 cleavage site is made uncleavable, sperm keep binding even after fertilization and cortical granule exocytosis. This placed the **ZP2 N-terminus**, and its cleavage, at the center of zona specificity and of the zona block.

When the acrosome reaction happens has also been revised. Jin et al. (2011), imaging transgenic mouse sperm in vivo, showed that most fertilizing sperm had already reacted before contacting the zona, often in the cumulus. Reacted sperm can still penetrate the zona and fertilize. The textbook idea that the zona induces the reaction is therefore at best incomplete. Progesterone acting through CatSper (via the lipid hydrolase ABHD2) and local calcium signaling are candidate triggers.

**Fusion machinery.** Inoue et al. (2005) identified IZUMO1, and Bianchi et al. (2014) identified its egg receptor, JUNO. Knockout mice lacking either protein are infertile because sperm reach the egg membrane but do not fuse. Neither protein looks like a fusogen. Additional sperm factors (SPACA6, TMEM95, FIMP, SOF1, DCST1/2) are each required for fusion, and their true fusogenic activity remains unresolved. CD9 organizes microvilli on the egg membrane.

**Activation.** PLCζ (Saunders et al., 2002) diffuses from the sperm perinuclear theca into the egg. It hydrolyzes PIP2 to IP3, which opens IP3 receptor type 1 channels in the endoplasmic reticulum. Calcium then oscillates for hours. CaMKIIγ activates EMI2 degradation, releasing the anaphase-promoting complex (APC/C). APC/C destroys cyclin B and securin, which ends metaphase II arrest. The pattern of oscillations affects later development.

**Polyspermy prevention** in mammals rests on ovastacin-mediated ZP2 cleavage and on JUNO shedding in extracellular vesicles within about 30-40 minutes. Unlike sea urchins and frogs, mammals have no significant electrical block. Dispermic zygotes form three pronuclei and usually arise as triploid or mosaic conceptuses.
levels.expert:
Clinically, the steps of fertilization map directly onto the techniques of assisted reproduction and the failures seen in the IVF lab.

**ICSI** (intracytoplasmic sperm injection) skips capacitation, zona penetration, the acrosome reaction and IZUMO1-JUNO fusion entirely. It does not skip egg activation, which still depends on sperm PLCζ. **Globozoospermia**, caused by DPY19L2 deletions or SPATA16 and PICK1 variants, produces round-headed sperm without an acrosome and often with deficient PLCζ. These cases, and PLCZ1-mutant men, explain many instances of total fertilization failure after ICSI. **Assisted oocyte activation** with calcium ionophores can rescue some cycles. Its long-term safety and the right patients to offer it to are still debated, because ionophores produce a single calcium rise rather than physiological oscillations.

Egg-side genetics are emerging. Variants in **ZP1, ZP2 and ZP3** cause zona-free or thin-zona oocytes and infertility. **TUBB8** mutations cause meiotic arrest. **PATL2** and **WEE2** variants impair oocyte maturation and exit from meiosis after fertilization. Inherited **ASTL (ovastacin)** dysfunction is predicted to disturb the zona block. Assessing polyspermy matters practically. Three pronuclei (3PN) on day 1 after conventional IVF usually means dispermy, and these embryos are discarded. After ICSI, 3PN more often reflects failure to extrude the second polar body (digynic triploidy).

At the population level, dispermic and digynic triploidy account for a meaningful share of first-trimester miscarriages. **Diandric triploidy** underlies partial hydatidiform mole. Dispermy into an empty oocyte is one route to complete mole.

**Research frontiers:**
- Structural studies of IZUMO1-JUNO and of a sperm complex involving TMEM81, SPACA6 and IZUMO1 are being used to identify the true fusogen.
- AlphaFold-guided screens have proposed a ternary sperm complex involving TMEM81, which is predicted to form a trimer with the sperm proteins IZUMO1 and SPACA6.
- **Non-hormonal contraceptives** are being investigated, including JUNO-IZUMO1 blockers, CatSper inhibitors, soluble-adenylyl-cyclase inhibitors (TDI-11861 works for hours in mice) and ZP2-based approaches.

A lasting caution is that species matter. Mouse findings about where the acrosome reaction happens and which ZP protein acts as the receptor do not always transfer to humans. Human ZP4, which mice lack, also contributes to sperm binding.

keyPoints: Fertilization usually occurs in the ampulla of the uterine tube
The acrosome reaction releases enzymes like acrosin and exposes IZUMO1
ZP2's N-terminus is key for human sperm binding to the zona pellucida
IZUMO1 on sperm binds JUNO on the egg to enable fusion
Sperm PLC zeta triggers calcium oscillations that activate the egg and finish meiosis II
Polyspermy is blocked by ovastacin cleaving ZP2 and by JUNO shedding

test.q: Where in the female tract does fertilization usually take place?
test.explain: The ampulla, the widest part of the uterine tube, is the usual site. Implantation, not fertilization, happens in the uterine lining.

test.q: The acrosome is best described as:
choices: A mitochondrial sheath in the midpiece
A ring of follicle cells around the egg
A coat of glycoproteins on the egg
A Golgi-derived vesicle full of enzymes
test.explain: The acrosome caps the sperm head and is derived from the Golgi. The glycoprotein coat on the egg is the zona pellucida.

test.q: Which sperm protein binds JUNO on the egg membrane?
test.explain: IZUMO1, exposed after the acrosome reaction, binds the egg's JUNO receptor. Mice lacking either protein are infertile.

test.q: Which zona protein's N-terminus is now thought essential for human sperm binding?
test.explain: Genetic studies showed that the ZP2 N-terminus mediates sperm binding. This revised the older model in which ZP3 was the receptor.

test.q: What triggers calcium oscillations in the egg after fusion?
test.explain: PLC zeta delivered by the sperm makes IP3, which releases calcium from the endoplasmic reticulum in repeated waves.

test.q: Polyspermy usually produces a zygote that is:
test.explain: Two sperm plus the egg's set give three sets of chromosomes. Triploid embryos generally fail to develop.

test.q: How does the zona reaction stop additional sperm?
choices: Ovastacin cleaves ZP2 so sperm no longer bind
The egg membrane depolarizes for hours
The corona cells re-form a tight barrier
test.explain: Cortical granules release ovastacin, which cleaves ZP2. Mammals lack a significant electrical fast block.

test.q: Which event is a direct result of egg activation?
test.explain: Calcium oscillations release the egg from metaphase II arrest, and the second polar body is extruded. Capacitation and ovulation happen earlier.

test.q: Which sperm channel drives hyperactivated motility?
test.explain: CatSper is a sperm-specific calcium channel. The IP3 receptor sits on the egg's endoplasmic reticulum.

test.q: Small vesicles beneath the egg membrane that release enzymes after fertilization are called ___ granules.
test.explain: Exocytosis of the cortical granules modifies the zona pellucida so other sperm cannot bind.

test.q: What is the name of the main serine protease released from the acrosome?
test.explain: Acrosin, together with tail thrust, helps the sperm cut through the zona.

test.q: After fertilization, the egg and sperm nuclei are called ___ before they combine.
test.explain: The male and female pronuclei form after activation and then merge their chromosomes.

kidTest.q: How many sperm should get into the egg?
kidTest.explain: The egg needs one set of instructions from the dad.

kidTest.q: What does the bag on the sperm's head hold?
kidTest.explain: The bag holds tools that cut a path through the egg's wall.

kidTest.q: What happens to the egg's wall after one sperm gets in?
kidTest.explain: The hard wall works like a gate closing, so no other sperm can enter.

kidTest.q: Why would two sperm be a problem?
choices: The egg would be too tired
kidTest.explain: Two sets of dad's instructions are too many for the baby to grow properly.

kidTest.q: The tiny swimmers racing to the egg are called s _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: Sperm come from the dad and swim to the egg.

advancedTest.q: In mice with an uncleavable ZP2, sperm still bind the zona after fertilization. What does this show?
choices: Electrical depolarization is the main mammalian polyspermy block
Cortical granule exocytosis fails without ZP2 being present
ZP2 cleavage is central to the zona block to polyspermy
ZP3 glycans are the main block once fertilization has happened
advancedTest.explain: Cortical granules still release their contents, yet sperm keep binding. Cleavage of ZP2 itself must therefore be what makes the zona stop binding sperm.

advancedTest.q: Why can ICSI still fail with sperm lacking functional PLC zeta?
choices: The acrosome reaction has to happen inside the oocyte
Injected sperm are blocked from crossing the zona layer
JUNO is shed from the egg before injection takes place
Egg activation still needs sperm-driven calcium waves
advancedTest.explain: ICSI bypasses penetration and fusion but not activation. Activation depends on PLC zeta-driven calcium oscillations.

advancedTest.q: In vivo imaging found most fertilizing mouse sperm had reacted before reaching the zona. This most challenges:
choices: The idea that the zona induces the acrosome reaction
Calcium oscillations as the trigger for egg activation
The role of IZUMO1 in membrane fusion
The requirement for capacitation before fertilization
advancedTest.explain: If the reaction often happens in the cumulus, before zona contact, then zona binding cannot be its required trigger.

advancedTest.q: A 3PN zygote after ICSI, compared with 3PN after conventional IVF, more often reflects:
choices: Failure to extrude the second polar body
Dispermy from two injected sperm cells
Loss of the paternal pronucleus later on
Absence of the zona pellucida layer
advancedTest.explain: ICSI delivers only one sperm, so a third pronucleus usually comes from retained maternal chromosomes (digynic triploidy).

lessons.title: Cleavage, Compaction and Formation of the Morula

levels.kid:
After a sperm and an egg join, they make one special cell called a **zygote**. It is the very first cell of a whole new person!

Then the zygote starts to split. One cell becomes two. Two become four. Four become eight. This splitting is called **cleavage**.

Here is the funny part: the cells get smaller each time, like cutting a pizza into more and more slices. The whole ball stays the same size because it sits inside a clear shell.

After a few days, the cells squeeze together tightly, like friends in a group hug. Soon there are about 16 cells packed into a little ball. It looks a bit like a mulberry, so it is called a **morula**.
levels.hs:
After fertilization, the single-celled **zygote** begins a series of rapid mitotic divisions called **cleavage** as it travels down the uterine (fallopian) tube toward the uterus.

Key features of cleavage:
- The cells produced are called **blastomeres**.
- The embryo does not grow during cleavage. It stays inside the **zona pellucida**, a protective glycoprotein shell, so each division makes the cells smaller.
- Human cleavage is slow compared with frogs or flies. The first division happens about 24 to 30 hours after fertilization, and later divisions take roughly half a day to a day each.
- Divisions are **asynchronous**, meaning not all cells divide at the same time, so you can briefly see 3, 5 or 7 cells.

Around the 8-cell stage (day 3), something important happens: **compaction**. The loose, grape-like blastomeres flatten against each other and stick tightly together using an adhesion protein called **E-cadherin**. The embryo turns into a smooth, tight ball.

By about day 3 to 4, there are 12 to 32 cells, and the embryo is called a **morula**, from the Latin for mulberry. It usually enters the uterus around this time.

A real example: in IVF clinics, embryologists watch embryos through a microscope and grade them by cell number and how evenly they divide. Embryos that cleave on schedule tend to do better.
levels.college:
**Cleavage** is a series of mitotic divisions without overall growth that partitions the large zygote cytoplasm into progressively smaller blastomeres. Total embryo volume stays roughly constant inside the **zona pellucida** (ZP1, ZP2, ZP3, ZP4 glycoproteins in humans), so the nucleus-to-cytoplasm ratio rises with each division.

**Pattern in mammals:**
- **Holoblastic** (complete) division, because mammalian eggs have very little yolk.
- **Rotational cleavage**: at the second division, one blastomere divides meridionally and the other equatorially.
- **Asynchronous** divisions, so odd cell numbers appear.
- Slow timing: about 2 cells at day 1-1.5, 4 cells around day 2, 8 cells around day 3.

**Maternal-to-zygotic transition (MZT).** Early cleavage runs on maternal mRNAs and proteins stored in the oocyte. These are progressively degraded while the embryonic genome switches on, called **embryonic genome activation (EGA)**. In humans, the major wave of EGA occurs at the 4-to-8-cell stage. In mice it happens much earlier, at the 2-cell stage. Embryos that fail EGA arrest.

**Compaction (~8-cell stage, day 3):**
- Blastomeres maximize contact and flatten, driven by **E-cadherin**-mediated adherens junctions and actomyosin contractility.
- Cells become **polarized**: the outward-facing (apical) surface develops microvilli and an apical domain containing PAR3/PAR6/aPKC, while basolateral surfaces face neighbours.
- Tight junctions begin forming between outer cells, foreshadowing a sealed epithelium.

**Morula (~16-32 cells, day 3-4).** Polarization and subsequent divisions create two populations:
- **Outer cells**: polarized, which will become trophectoderm (future placenta).
- **Inner cells**: apolar, which will become the inner cell mass (future embryo).

This **inside-outside** distinction is the first cell-fate decision. Fluid accumulation then converts the morula into a blastocyst, which is covered in the next unit.
levels.phd:
Cleavage-stage biology is dominated by three problems: running development on a maternal dowry, activating the embryonic genome, and breaking symmetry to set the first lineage decision.

**Maternal control and EGA.** Oocyte-derived transcripts drive the first divisions; their clearance involves both maternal decay pathways and zygotically dependent decay. In humans, a minor transcriptional wave occurs at the 1-2-cell stage, and the major wave occurs at 4-8 cells (Braude, Bolton and Moore, 1988, showed that α-amanitin-sensitive transcription is required by this stage). Pioneer and pluripotency-associated factors are implicated, including **DUX4** (driving a 2-cell-like/8-cell-like program) and **TPRX1/2**, together with extensive chromatin remodelling and global DNA demethylation of the parental genomes (active TET3-mediated oxidation for the paternal genome, largely passive dilution for the maternal genome).

**Compaction mechanics.** Compaction is not just adhesion. Maître et al. (2015) showed that increased cortical tension at cell-medium interfaces, generated by actomyosin and moderated by E-cadherin at contacts, drives blastomere flattening. Maternal E-cadherin (Cdh1) is sufficient for compaction in mice; maternal-zygotic knockouts fail to compact.

**Symmetry breaking and the inside-outside model.** Tarkowski and Wroblewska's inside-outside hypothesis (1967) and Johnson and Ziomek's polarization model (1981) are now unified by molecular data:
- Apical PAR-aPKC domains in outer cells sequester **angiomotin (Amot)**, keeping **Hippo** signalling (LATS1/2) inactive. Unphosphorylated **YAP** enters the nucleus, binds **TEAD4** and activates **Cdx2** and **Gata3** for trophectoderm.
- In apolar inner cells, Amot at adherens junctions activates LATS, YAP is phosphorylated and kept in the cytoplasm, and **Sox2** remains expressed for the inner cell mass (Nishioka et al., 2009).
- Asymmetric (differentiative) divisions of polarized cells, along with cell sorting by tension differences, determine how many cells are internalized.

**Controversy:** whether mouse blastomeres show fate bias as early as the 4-cell stage (e.g., CARM1-mediated H3R26 methylation and Sox21) remains debated. Human data diverge from mouse: human TE specification appears to use polarity-YAP-GATA3 but with different timing, and human embryos compact later and less uniformly.
levels.expert:
For clinicians and embryologists, the cleavage stage is where most early human embryonic loss originates, and where assisted reproduction intervenes most directly.

**Chromosomal mosaicism.** Human cleavage is strikingly error-prone. Aneuploidy in cleavage-stage embryos is common even in young, fertile patients, and much of it is **mitotic** rather than meiotic: chaotic mosaicism, tripolar divisions and micronuclei. A plausible contributor is that early human blastomeres have weak spindle assembly checkpoint function and rely on centrosomes inherited from the sperm. Time-lapse imaging shows that **direct cleavage** (one cell to three) and **reverse cleavage** predict poorer outcomes, and multinucleation is a common warning sign.

**Embryo assessment in IVF.**
- Traditional day-3 grading uses blastomere number, symmetry and fragmentation percentage. Fragmentation partly reflects micronuclei and apoptotic blebs.
- Most clinics now prefer extended culture to day 5 blastocyst, selecting embryos that survived EGA and compaction.
- **Time-lapse morphokinetics** (e.g., timing of the 2-, 3-, 5- and 8-cell stages and of compaction) feeds AI ranking models. Randomized trials have not shown consistent live-birth benefit, a key open question.

**Biopsy and PGT-A.** Day-3 single-blastomere biopsy was largely abandoned because one cell poorly represents a mosaic embryo and removal impaired development. Trophectoderm biopsy at the blastocyst stage replaced it, but mosaic PGT-A results still create real counselling dilemmas, since some mosaic embryos yield healthy births, possibly through selective elimination of aneuploid cells.

**Totipotency and fate.** Individual 2-cell and 4-cell blastomeres can retain broad developmental potential, which explains why monozygotic twinning can arise from splitting at cleavage stages (covered in the twinning unit). Hatching from the zona pellucida comes later; early zona damage can also predispose to splitting.

**Frontiers.** Stem-cell-derived **8-cell-like cells** and blastoids are being used to model EGA and compaction without embryos, raising regulatory questions about the 14-day rule. Single-cell multi-omics is mapping when human lineage bias first appears, still unresolved.

keyPoints: Cleavage is rapid mitosis without growth inside the zona pellucida
Blastomeres get smaller with each division; human divisions are slow and asynchronous
Embryonic genome activation occurs at the 4-8-cell stage in humans
Compaction at about 8 cells uses E-cadherin and cortical tension
Outer polarized cells become trophectoderm; inner apolar cells become inner cell mass
The morula (~16-32 cells, day 3-4) enters the uterus

test.q: Why do blastomeres get smaller with each cleavage division?
choices: The embryo does not grow inside the zona pellucida
Each division discards half the yolk stores
The cells lose water to the surrounding fluid
Meiosis halves the chromosome number each time
test.explain: Cleavage partitions a fixed volume of cytoplasm inside the zona, so cells shrink. It is mitosis, not meiosis.

test.q: Around which stage does compaction begin in the human embryo?
test.explain: Compaction begins around the 8-cell stage on about day 3.

test.q: Which adhesion protein is central to compaction?
test.explain: E-cadherin forms adherens junctions that let blastomeres flatten and stick together.

test.q: Mammalian cleavage is holoblastic mainly because the egg:
test.explain: Little yolk allows complete division of the whole egg.

test.q: In humans, the major wave of embryonic genome activation occurs at about the:
test.explain: Humans activate their genome strongly at 4-8 cells; mice do so at the 2-cell stage.

test.q: Why can a human embryo briefly have 3, 5 or 7 cells?
choices: Extra cells enter from the tube
test.explain: Blastomeres do not all divide at the same moment, so odd numbers appear.

test.q: Outer, polarized cells of the morula will mainly form the:
test.explain: Outer polarized cells become trophectoderm, the future placenta; inner cells form the inner cell mass.

test.q: Early cleavage divisions are driven mostly by:
test.explain: Before genome activation, the embryo relies on maternal products stored in the oocyte.

test.q: Roughly when does the morula form and reach the uterus?
test.explain: The morula of about 12-32 cells forms around day 3-4 and enters the uterus about then.

test.q: What are the cells produced by cleavage called?
test.explain: Each cell made by cleavage divisions is a blastomere.

test.q: The name morula comes from the Latin word for ___.
test.explain: The tightly packed ball of cells resembles a mulberry.

test.q: The glycoprotein shell around the cleaving embryo is the zona ___.
test.explain: The zona pellucida surrounds the embryo until hatching.

kidTest.q: What is the very first cell of a new person called?
kidTest.explain: The zygote forms when sperm and egg join.

kidTest.q: What happens to the cells as they keep splitting?
kidTest.explain: Like pizza slices, they get smaller because the ball stays the same size.

kidTest.q: What do the cells do around the 8-cell stage?
kidTest.explain: They squeeze together like a group hug. This is compaction.

kidTest.q: Why is the ball called a morula?
choices: It is very hard like a rock
kidTest.explain: Morula means mulberry, and the ball of cells looks like one.

kidTest.q: The splitting of the first cell into many cells is called c _ _ _ _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: Cleavage means the cell splits again and again.

advancedTest.q: A mouse embryo lacking both maternal and zygotic E-cadherin would most likely show:
choices: Premature hatching from the zona pellucida
Normal compaction but no genome activation
Failure to compact and disrupted lineage sorting
advancedTest.explain: E-cadherin is required for compaction; without it, flattening and the junction-dependent inside-outside signals fail.

advancedTest.q: In an inner apolar blastomere, which state best explains Sox2 expression?
choices: Nuclear YAP bound to TEAD4 driving Cdx2
Strong cortical tension causing outward cell sorting
Apical aPKC sequestering angiomotin away from junctions
Active LATS phosphorylating YAP so it stays cytoplasmic
advancedTest.explain: Junctional angiomotin activates Hippo/LATS, YAP is retained in the cytoplasm, TEAD4 targets stay off, and Sox2 persists.

advancedTest.q: Why was day-3 single-blastomere biopsy largely replaced by trophectoderm biopsy?
choices: One cell poorly represents a mosaic embryo and removal harmed development
Trophectoderm cells later form the fetus, giving direct information
Embryonic genome activation destroys DNA in biopsied cells
Blastomeres contain no nuclear DNA at day 3
advancedTest.explain: High mitotic mosaicism makes a single blastomere unrepresentative, and removing a cell from an 8-cell embryo impaired development.

advancedTest.q: A human embryo cultured with a transcription inhibitor from fertilization would be expected to arrest around:
choices: The blastocyst stage, after the trophectoderm forms
The 4-8-cell stage, when zygotic genes are needed
The first division, since early proteins are mostly zygotic
Gastrulation, when the first signaling centers appear
advancedTest.explain: Maternal mRNAs and proteins drive the earliest cleavages. In human embryos, embryonic genome activation becomes essential around the 4-8-cell stage, so transcription-blocked embryos arrest there, as Braude and colleagues showed. Mouse embryos activate their genome earlier and arrest at the 2-cell stage.
